sections.text: But, O Arjuna! All honour to him whose mind controls his senses, for he is thereby beginning to practise Karma-Yoga, the Path of Right Action, keeping himself always unattached.
नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः।
Do thy duty as prescribed, for action for dutys sake is superior to inaction. Even the maintenance of the body would be impossible if man remained inactive.
In this world people are fettered by action, unless it is performed as a sacrifice. Therefore, O Arjuna, let thy acts be done without attachment, as sacrifice only.

So far we have seen the dilemma of whether to work in this world or renounce actions. We have discussed many times that action -- which is an interaction between I and this world -- creates impressions. These impressions on my mind create tendencies, these tendencies create desires, the desires create actions.
And then the cycle starts all over again. The more I act, the more I interact with this world. That interaction will have this cause and effect relationship.
This cycle seems like never ending cycle that I can never get out of this. And the whole purpose of all this studies is to get out of this cycle. So obviously Arjuna is confused whether he should act by fighting this war or renounce all these actions and go to Himalaya.
So thats where we started the chapter. In the last verse, we have seen Bhagavan say Niyatam Kuru Karmatvam -- a very firm prescription. You must do all your ordained duties.
Niyatam Kuru Karmatvam Karma Jayahi Akarma Naha Because Karma is superior than inaction. Action is superior than inaction. So very simple, very clear that what you should do in life is do your ordained duties.
And, and we have seen in last discussion, the ordained duties are. Daily duties which we cant really escape. Brushing your teeth, taking bath, going to work, all these Nitya Karma, theres nothing special about it.
Nobody is going to congratulate you every morning for brushing your teeth, unless you are a little three-year-old child. Then there is Naimittya Karma, which are the special duties -- when something is required by your family, your community, your society, your nation, then you have to perform those duties. Youre not doing those duties every day.
On special occasions youre required to participate. Either you have a voluntary army or a draft. If youre not volunteering on your own to protect your country, there will be a draft.
You have to draft you because thats required a special duty. So Bhagavan says Niyyatam Kuru Karma Tvam. Niyata Karma includes both the Nitya and Naimittya -- that means there is no escape from any duty.
Your friend is sick and he needs your help. At that time you can say, I am very busy. You can, but that means you are shirking your duty. You are not doing your part.
So Bhagawan very clearly says Nidham Kuru Karma Thomas Karma Jyay or Karmanaha Karma is anytime better than inaction. Action is anytime better than inaction. Sari Yatra Apicha Tena prasiddayat or Karmanah.
By inaction you cant even sustain your body. We can understand that even to sustain my body, I have to act. And therefore action is prescribed here.
So now we are still in the conundrum. On one hand we want to liberate ourselves from this bondage and other hand we have to act. So it looks like catch 22.
So the next four verses, are laid out as the overall scheme of thing as the Creator has created how to act and how to be liberated from your actions, not bound by your actions. Also, when this world is created, there should be a plan for sustaining it. So the whole plan is laid out in the next few verses.
And I obviously had been listening to from the Cold War era. Used to say, Dont blame me or dont put me in jail because it sounds like Im a communist or a socialist. Krishna is the socialist, not me. Where Krishna now lays out the whole path of socialism in the next four verses, there is no real socialist nation on this planet, because even in communist countries, there are people who are just in it for their power.
Thats not what the socialism is all about. So the next four verses lay out the whole plan of sustaining this universe and you being a part of that universe. How you can participate but not get bound by your actions.
So the next verse says, Yajnar Thaat Karmano anyatra Loko Ayam Karma Bandanaha. Actions other than those performed for the Yajna are binding Loko yam in this loka in this world. This Loka is bound by Kun, cause and effect.
Everything in this world is bound by cause and effect. There is nothing in this world that is free from cause and effect. Therefore, we give this standard example.
If I see something in this room, its an effect. If I see a table in this room, its an effect. And I cannot say that this table has no cause.
Where did this table come? Kneel and say, we are chinma mission, we dont want to do anything. And table appears here. Obviously nobody will believe me because you know I bought it from somewhere.
Even if I didnt buy it, I stole it from somebody. So buy, borrow or steal. Only three ways we can acquire things.
Table is in effect, so it must have a cause. This cause has two aspects, efficient cause and a material cause. Someone who knew how to make this table is the efficient cause carpenter and the material cause, the wood which was required.
So having this relationship of cause and effect, this table comes into existence. So in this loca everything is bound by cause and effect. So if you act, there will be an effect.
So you will be bound by this cause and effect. If you are acting for your own desires, for your own betterment, for your own good only. But if you are working for the betterment of the whole society, for the cosmic order, then you are bound by one thing.
So yajna karmano van Yatra, actions performed for the Yajna. Obviously we know culturally that its a ritual of offering sacrifices in the fire. But the original meaning, the significance of Yajna in the Vedic period, was to propitiate the deities who are in charge of these elemental forces.
As an observant person, we realize that there are two aspects of my success. One is my own efforts, but then also the environment in which Im putting my efforts. I may be a very hard-working farmer, but if there is no rain, obviously I will not have any success.
So I know that something other than me is participating in my success. Thats what we call Devam. Thats something destiny we call it.
So these phenomenal forces are the ones I dont have control over. One year there is a lot of rain, the other year there is a drought and third year there is just appropriate rain. How do I control that? There must be some controller who decides this.
That controller we call deva. Maybe there is a controller who controls this rain, a deva. So if we appease those devas, it will be good for the whole society and there will be rain for the whole society.
This yajnas were the cooperative endeavor to appease the deities of phenomenal forces. So the purpose was to have a common good where everyone can benefit in the community. Therefore you hear the story about in Bhagavad, Krishna lifting the govardhan parvat.
You know how it all started. Krishna was a reformer. Everybody was doing yajna to Indra.
Krishna said, Why are you offering this Yajna to Indra? Indra is not doing anything for you. These cows are supporting you. This Mother Earth is supporting you. Lets have Yajna for the cows and lay Yajna for the earth.
Thats from Mother Earth. Mother Cow, they are supporting us, not Indra. So Indra got mad and then the whole story goes he sent all the storms and hurricanes and typhoons or whatever.
And then Krishna protects them under the Govardhan Parvat. Even though he was holding it, everyone else was supporting it with their sticks. And then in the end what do we have? Because of the rain, theres so much food that when all the rains subsided, everybody said lets have a party.
Everybody brought their own food. So there was Annakut. There was like the mountain of food.
So if you think that potluck was started in America, Krishna started potluck from that Govardhan Parvat there. So the whole idea is that we have a capacity to work together for the common good. When we work together for common good that include my good also.
But not just my good, but everyone elses good as well. Those actions are considered Yajna actions. Bhagavan says all the actions performed in that spirit are not binding.
You may be acting in your profession, but if youre only acting for the salary, then thats a selfish action. But acting because you are improving other peoples lives -- by participating as a doctor, as an engineer, youre making the society better and making everyones life easier -- thats Yajna action. Actions performed in the spirit of Yajna are non-binding.
All others are binding. So here is your escape hatch. You can continue doing whatever you are doing.
Just change the attitude that Im not doing it for myself, Im doing it for the greater good. Whether Im an architect, a doctor, a housewife, a mother, everything Im doing is not just for me but for the overall good of the society, the community, the cosmos, the universe. So Yajna Karmano Anyatna Loko Yam Karma Bandanah Tadartam Karma Kantaya Mukta Sangha Samacharah.
Therefore here is the clear advice. Perform actions in the Yajna spirit for Yajna without any attachment. Perform your actions.
Nothing you have to change in your life. Purely your attitude towards your actions. Im doing these actions because it will help the Entire society.
Therefore we have this now new awareness about green buildings, green society, energy savings. None of this is new -- we had it in our culture. Therefore when I go for my presentations on this green initiative, I say well, I never had to learn because it comes from my culture.
We respected the mother earth, we respected nature because we understood those Vedic people understood the value of nature and our participation. Therefore Bhagavan says Tadartam Karma Kaunteya -- act for the Yajna. Therefore act for Yajna only, Mukta Sangha, without attachment.
Not having the attachment that I am the doer. I am the only one who can do this. Because you are just a part of the whole society.
You are not an island by yourself. By yourself you are worthy of doing nothing. Just simple act of me coming to this class, I cannot do by myself.
So many people have to do so many things. Police have to make sure that there are no crimes on the road. Roads are clear, the traffic is properly regulated.
BMW has to make a car so I can drive a car. Gas companies have to put the gas in the gas stations. All that when it all come together, I can make the simple move from my house to within center if I recognize that.
Bhagavan said you are Mukta Sangha. You are detached from your actions. Sahayagnaha Prajaha Srishtva Purow Vacha Prajapati.
How did all this start? Bhagavan says the Creator, when he created this universe, knew that he has to sustain it. If we create something and we do not know how to sustain it -- say we start a business -- we need to know how to sustain the business. If you start any endeavor or create any creation, you have to make sure you maintain it, you sustain it.
So you have to have a plan for that. You have painting artists create. You have to have a plan for how you are going to protect it, where you are going to display it, how to preserve it.
So there is always a plan for sustaining something when you create it. Therefore, in Hindu trinity there is a creator, a sustainer and a destroyer.

Here Krishna introduces one of the Gitas most transformative concepts: Yajna, or sacrifice. The word transforms our understanding of action entirely. Actions performed for selfish gain bind us to the wheel of karma, creating an endless cycle of cause and effect. But actions performed as Yajna - as an offering to the greater good - do not bind. This is the escape hatch Krishna offers: you need not change what you do, only the spirit in which you do it.
Consider the profound statement: Niyatam kuru karma tvam - do your prescribed duty. Even maintaining the body requires action. You cannot survive without eating, and eating requires the action of procuring food. The question is never whether to act, but how. When you work only for salary, you are bound by that transaction. When you work recognizing that your profession serves others - that the doctor heals, the teacher enlightens, the architect creates shelter - the same action becomes Yajna.
Today, take your most mundane task - perhaps cooking a meal, answering emails, or commuting to work - and consciously reframe it as Yajna. Ask yourself: How does this action serve something larger than my personal gain? How can I offer this task as a sacrifice rather than perform it as a transaction? Notice how this shift in attitude, without changing the action itself, changes your experience of doing it. The action remains; the bondage dissolves.
